draft.title: Empirical and molecular formulas
card: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule. It is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

To find the empirical formula, take the mass of each element, such as from percentage composition in a 100 g sample. Divide each by its molar mass to get moles, then divide all by the smallest number of moles.
To find the molecular formula, divide the compound's molar mass by the empirical formula's molar mass. Multiply the empirical formula by this whole number.
draft.remember: Percentage composition gives the ratio. Molar mass gives the multiple.

a.q: A compound has the empirical formula CH2O and a molar mass of 180 g/mol. The empirical formula mass is 30 g/mol. What is its molecular formula?
a.why: 180 ÷ 30 = 6, so multiply every subscript in CH2O by 6 to get C6H12O6. C3H6O3 would be a multiple of 3, which gives only 90 g/mol.
a.clue: How many times does the empirical mass fit into the molar mass?

b.q: A compound is 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. Its molar mass is 56 g/mol. Use C = 12 and H = 1. What is its molecular formula?
b.why: In 100 g: C = 85.7 ÷ 12 = 7.14 mol and H = 14.3 ÷ 1 = 14.3 mol. The ratio is 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH2, with mass 14 g/mol. 56 ÷ 14 = 4, giving C4H8. CH2 is only the ratio, not the actual molecule.
b.clue: Find the ratio first, then scale it up using the molar mass.

check.summary: No problems found. Both calculations check out (180 ÷ 30 = 6 gives C6H12O6; a 1:2 ratio gives CH2, and 56 ÷ 14 = 4 gives C4H8), and the card, remember line and explanations are accurate.
